For continuous, twice-differentiable functions, we can determine possible points of inflection by solving the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$ However, we must be sure to check that the concavity does indeed change at whatever points we find.

First, we calculate the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}{e}^{-1/{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}){e}^{-1/{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}){e}^{-1/{x}^{2}} \\  & =(-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{4}{{x}^{6}}){e}^{-1/{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{6}}\,(2-3{x}^{2})\,{e}^{-1/{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve ${f}^{″}(x)=0,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{{x}^{6}}(2-3{x}^{2}){e}^{-1/{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 2-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we ignored the negative square root since $x\in (0,\infty ).$

Finally, we need to check if the concavity changes at $x=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}.$ So, we pick two points around it, say $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=1$, and compute the sign of ${f}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}\,(\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{2}{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{6}}\,(2-3\,{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}){e}^{-1/(1/2)^{2}} \\  & =128\,(2-\frac{3}{4}){e}^{-4} \\  & =160{e}^{-4}>0 \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =\frac{2}{1}\,(2-3)\,{e}^{-1} \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}<0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the concavity changes at $x=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}},$ we conclude that $x=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$ is indeed a point of inflection.
